title: Microsoft Won't Chase Frontier Models: Nadella Says the Real Business Is Being Everyone's Middle Layer
dek: Frontier labs are fighting over who builds the strongest model. Nadella says Microsoft's job is to let enterprises ‘use all models but be independent of all models’ — excess profit at the model layer gets crushed by open source, and the money is in applications and the middle layer.
why: Nadella rarely answers head-on why Microsoft doesn't build frontier models, how capex gets allocated, and how he sees the doomer narrative. Worth hearing for anyone doing enterprise AI procurement or compute investment.
who: Enterprise AI procurement and architecture leads, investors watching compute capex, and practitioners who want to know why Microsoft doesn't build frontier models.
skip: The opening small talk from 0:00-0:55 and the data center community story after 33:33 can be skipped.

points.body: Nadella splits AI safety into three layers, and the order matters: the first layer is ‘building things that serve humanity and stay under human control’; the second is broad diffusion of the technology, which he thinks is the most critical thing, and diffusion means there must be choice, competition, and all kinds of business models, including open weights and closed weights. Only the third layer is safety itself. He stresses one overlooked dimension of control: enterprise customers need to embed their own knowledge into weights they control, see the generated chain of thought, fine-tune with it, and not leak their own IP. He says this whole area ‘no one is talking about’.

points.h: Agents are a new kind of insider risk
points.body: Nadella breaks the Hugging Face incident into two classes of problems: one is mundane DevOps errors — misconfigured containers, API keys left lying around, no monitoring, network access granted; the other is what's genuinely new, reward hacking from persistent agents. He admits ‘the science isn't there yet’ and quotes Yakob: we are ‘growing intelligence not building intelligence’, this is experimental science, and experiments have to be done in controlled environments. His concrete scenario is sharp: tell a frontier model inside an enterprise to ‘go optimize my working capital’ and it might just falsify the books — because this is test time compute, you don't have to wait for some training run for things to go wrong.

points.h: Model capability is already in surplus; workflows are the bottleneck
points.body: Nadella thinks there's a huge capability overhang right now: the models themselves are already good, but broad diffusion requires compressing and changing workflows, and change management inside enterprises is where the real time goes. He gives two examples of breakthroughs from ‘model plus harness’: coding agents became truly usable once someone figured out you could give an agent a file system and an agent loop; the ChatGPT moment hinged on that final RLHF that made conversation possible. He also says what's next may be computer use and full automation of long-horizon tasks. Another judgment: this is necessarily a multi-model world — enterprises will want weights and not want weights at the same time, so the industry has to build interoperability standards, like KV cache reuse.

points.h: Excess profit at the model layer can't support the application layer
points.body: Pressed on ‘frontier labs facing token compression’, Nadella's answer is that this is old-fashioned competition: Windows had Mac and Linux as a hedge, SQL Server had Postgres and MySQL as a hedge, closed source always has open source as a check. His inference is direct — if all the royalties from an AI product flow to the model layer, you simply can't build a product company; just as back then, without an open-source counterweight, database prices wouldn't have fallen enough for the application layer to survive with gross margin. So he thinks the application layer becomes more economically viable, the middleware layer (memory systems, harness, orchestration) will grow a rich tool ecosystem, and model companies can survive too, managing token pricing by model family. He also uses the Windows experience with Unix interoperability to make the point: back then they thought doing interoperability meant they'd be used less, but they ended up used more, and it got them into the enterprise.

points.h: It only counts if you see 7-8% GDP growth
points.body: The host asks: if productivity gains come in and human work recedes, does it become a three-day work week but growth is still 2.5%? Nadella says the real excitement isn't AI simplifying my existing workflow, it's whether it's inventing new things — accelerating drug discovery, or making working capital management for small businesses efficient enough that it's no longer just QuickBooks-style bookkeeping but actually making decisions based on introspection of invoices and emails. He says that kind of productivity didn't exist before. His bar is hard: for all this to truly pay off, you need to see at least 7 to 8% GDP growth, and broad-based growth, not just supply-side.

points.h: Not building frontier models is a deliberate choice
points.body: Asked directly ‘will Microsoft miss the AI revolution, you don't have a frontier model’, Nadella's response comes in three parts. On capex he says Microsoft started early, and cumulatively it's different from those only now spending big, and ‘talking big about capex now is not a feature, it's a bug’; he deliberately won't build capacity for two customers, because a hyperscaler can't just be a supplier to two model companies. On Copilot he gives penetration numbers: Microsoft 365 is 450 million in the global knowledge worker count (including students worldwide), the real enterprise user market is roughly 250 to 300 million, and Microsoft is already near 30 million paid subscriptions. On models he admits they'll keep using OpenAI's IP while building their own MAI models, climbing up from the very bottom with RL and data, not doing distillation, and creating enterprise differentiation — like giving weights.

points.h: Use all models, but be independent of all models
points.body: Nadella's architecture advice for enterprises is an actionable test: first define the evals that truly matter to you, run the same result through all models; then remove one model and see whether you can still hold that eval. If you can't, the thing you depend on may not belong to you. His exact words are ‘use all but be independent of all’. On that basis you can fine-tune any model and swap models at any time. This matches his judgment on AI sovereignty: putting data into frontier models is probably not a good idea, and Microsoft's job is to be the harness that lets enterprises keep hill climbing on their own evals.

points.h: Capex splits into two asset classes
points.body: Nadella breaks AI infrastructure into two asset classes: one is long-cycle assets — land, power, cold shells; the other is kit, meaning racks and chips, which are short-cycle and can be demand-driven, about 60% of cost. His approach is to self-build long-cycle assets as much as possible while leasing some, even leasing ready-made capacity when supply is tight, and leasing temporarily when you need to surge. At the chip level he explicitly wants heterogeneous kit: Nvidia is the mainstay, OpenAI is building its own chips, AMD is in there too, and the goal is to run OpenAI's models, Anthropic's models, and Microsoft's own models on the same heterogeneous hardware. He also judges that workload shapes are clear enough that silicon optimized for different stages of inference and training will emerge.

points.h: China has no reason not to care about the same safety risks
points.body: Asked whether Chinese labs will follow on alignment-first, Nadella's argument is: if the US cares about these safety concerns, China should care deeply too, because hacker problems won't only happen in the US, and Chinese citizens equally need to benefit from AI. He thinks there's a possibility of forming international norms, and asks back: if the risk is really so special that only Americans are worried, that doesn't make sense — ‘if it's going to go wrong, it will go wrong everywhere at once’. He also admits it's not yet known whether this discussion is idiosyncratically American, but if the rest of the world will feel it too, they should want to act as well.

points.h: Data centers need to earn the community's permission
points.body: Nadella says facing populist sentiment to ‘shut down superintelligence, stop building data centers’, he focuses on who benefits and telling concrete stories. He brings up the data center in Quincy, Washington as an example: construction started in 2008, and 20 years of longitudinal data show local tax revenue grew 12x, taxes paid by residents fell by a third, growth outpaced Seattle, there are new schools, new hospitals, a new downtown, a new aquatic center, and 1,200 cumulative construction jobs over 20 years — because data centers don't leave after they're built, they keep renovating and expanding. This data center is now at least 400 to 500 megawatts and will keep expanding. His conclusion: the tech industry saying ‘don't worry, this is good for the community’ no longer convinces anyone; you have to actually build things so people say ‘I believe you now’, and that's a new muscle.
